title: What I Wish Someone Had Told Me: Sam Altman's 17 lessons on starting and finishing things
summary: A list of 17 compact lessons from Sam Altman on how companies get started and finished. He covers audacious goals, concentrating bets, recruiting, fast iteration, incentives, and building businesses with compounding advantages at scale.

principles.text: Pick a hard, meaningful problem: teams do it more easily than an easy, unimportant one.
principles.quote: It is easier for a team to do a hard thing that really matters than to do an easy thing that doesn’t really matter; audacious ideas motivate people.

principles.text: Concentrate resources on a few high-conviction bets and cut more than you think you can.
principles.quote: Concentrate your resources on a small number of high-conviction bets; this is easy to say but evidently hard to do. You can delete more stuff than you think.

principles.text: Plan long-term but iterate fast; speed makes up for being wrong.
principles.quote: Fast iteration can make up for a lot; it’s usually ok to be wrong if you iterate quickly. Plans should be measured in decades, execution should be measured in weeks.

principles.text: Spend more time recruiting; bet on high-potential, fast-improving people with evidence of getting things done.
principles.quote: Spend more time recruiting. Take risks on high-potential people with a fast rate of improvement. Look for evidence of getting stuff done in addition to intelligence.

principles.text: Judge by outcomes, and fight bureaucracy rather than letting process excuse bad results.
principles.quote: Outcomes are what count; don’t let good process excuse bad results.

principles.text: Build a business whose advantage compounds with scale.
principles.quote: Compounding exponentials are magic. In particular, you really want to build a business that gets a compounding advantage with scale.
